Mr. Wopsle’s stare grew so intense that it puzzled me. He seemed to be turning over several thoughts at once and getting more confused by the minute. Long after he had been lifted into the clouds in a giant watch case, I was still wondering what had happened. I had found no answer an hour later, when I left the theatre and discovered him waiting for me near the door.

“How are you?” I said. We shook hands and started down the street together. “I could see you had noticed me.”

“Noticed you, Mr. Pip!” he replied. “Yes, of course. But who else was there?”

“Who else?”

“It’s the most extraordinary thing,” said Mr. Wopsle, looking lost in thought again. “Yet I would swear I knew him.”

This began to frighten me, and I urged him to tell me what he meant.

“If you hadn’t been there, I might not have spotted him at first,” Mr. Wopsle went on, still seeming distracted. “I can’t be sure. But I think I would have.”

His strange remarks made me shiver. Instinctively I looked around, as I was used to doing when I walked home.

“Oh, he won’t be anywhere near us,” said Mr. Wopsle. “He left before I finished onstage. I saw him go.”

I had such good reason to be on my guard that I grew suspicious even of this poor actor. Perhaps he was trying to lure me into admitting something. I glanced at him as we continued walking, but did not answer.

“I had a silly idea that he must have been with you, Mr. Pip. Then I realised you hadn’t noticed him at all, sitting right behind you like a ghost.”

Again I felt that chill. Still, I refused to speak. His words might fit a plan to make me connect what he was saying with Provis. Someone could have put him up to it. Of course, I knew for certain that Provis had not been at the theatre.

“You must find me rather puzzling, Mr. Pip. I can see that you do. But this is so strange! You’ll find it hard to believe what I’m going to say. If you told me the same thing, I could hardly believe you.”

“Is that so?” I asked.

“Yes, indeed. Mr. Pip, do you remember that Christmas Day years ago, when you were a little boy? I had dinner at Gargery’s, and some soldiers came to get a pair of handcuffs fixed.”

“I remember it very well.”

“And do you remember how we joined the hunt for two escaped convicts? Gargery took you on his back, and I went ahead, and you followed as fast as you could?”

At last we agreed to share a dwelling for the duration of my visit to the city. As my finances were rather less constrained than his, he allowed me to bear the cost of renting and furnishing, in a manner agreeable to the somewhat fantastic melancholy we shared, an ancient and grotesque mansion. Long abandoned owing to superstitious fears we never investigated, it stood crumbling towards ruin in a secluded, forsaken quarter of the Faubourg St. Germain.

Had the world been acquainted with our daily habits there, it would have pronounced us mad, though perhaps harmlessly so. Our withdrawal was complete. Nobody visited us. Indeed, I had carefully concealed the location of our retreat from all my previous acquaintances, and Dupin had for many years neither known nor been known by anyone in Paris. We lived entirely within ourselves.

My friend had a caprice of imagination—what other name can I give it?—which made him love the night simply for herself. Into this eccentricity, as into his other singularities, I slipped without protest, surrendering wholly to his extravagant fancies. The dark goddess could not remain perpetually in our company, but we could imitate her presence. At the first hint of dawn we shut every disordered shutter of the old house and lit two candles, heavily scented, whose rays were exceedingly feeble and ghostly. In their light we occupied our spirits with dreams, reading, writing, or talking until the clock announced the arrival of genuine Darkness. Then, arm in arm, we ventured into the streets, pursuing the discussions of the day or wandering far afield until a late hour. Among the strange lights and shadows of the crowded city we sought the boundless stimulation that the mind may derive from tranquil observation.

On these occasions I could not but notice and admire Dupin’s extraordinary power of analysis, although the wealth of his imagination had led me to anticipate it. He seemed also to delight eagerly in using that faculty, if not precisely in exhibiting it, and readily admitted the satisfaction it afforded him. With a subdued chuckle he would boast that, so far as he was concerned, most men had windows set in their breasts. Such declarations were usually followed by immediate and astonishing demonstrations of his intimate acquaintance with my own heart. At these moments his bearing became cold and remote, his eyes expressionless, while his voice, ordinarily a rich tenor, climbed to a treble. It might have sounded peevish, had not his utterance been so deliberate and so perfectly distinct.

They were bringing along a mighty respectable-looking old gentleman, and a pleasant-looking younger one with his right arm in a sling. And goodness alive, how the crowd shouted and laughed, and wouldn’t stop! I couldn’t find the fun in it myself, and I reckoned the duke and the king would have a hard time finding any either. I expected them to go white. But no, they didn’t lose a speck of color. The duke never showed he guessed what was happening; he just kept bubbling along, pleased as could be, like buttermilk gurgling out of a jug. And the king kept looking down at those newcomers so sorrowfully you’d think the notion of such cheats existing gave him a stomachache right in his heart. Oh, he played it beautifully. A heap of the leading people crowded around him to show whose side they were on. The old gentleman who’d just arrived seemed utterly bewildered. When he finally spoke, I could tell at once he sounded like an Englishman—not the way the king did, though the king’s imitation was fairly good. I can’t repeat the gentleman’s language or copy his manner, but he faced the crowd and said something like this:

“This has taken me completely by surprise, and I frankly confess I’m poorly prepared to deal with it or answer it. My brother and I have suffered some misfortunes. His arm is broken, and last night our luggage was mistakenly unloaded at a town farther upriver. I’m Harvey, Peter Wilks’s brother, and this is his brother William. He can neither hear nor speak, and with only one hand available he can hardly even manage his signs. We are precisely who we claim to be. Once our baggage arrives, in a day or two, I can establish it. Until then I’ll say nothing further, but wait at the hotel.”

So he and the new deaf-and-dumb man set off, and the king laughed and bawled:

“Broken his arm—how very probable! And wonderfully handy for an impostor who needs to make signs and hasn’t learned them. Their baggage lost! That’s a fine one, and extremely clever under the circumstances!”

He laughed some more, and everybody joined him except three or four, or perhaps half a dozen. The doctor was one. Another was a shrewd-looking gentleman carrying one of those old carpetbags actually made from carpet, who had just stepped off the steamboat. He and the doctor were talking quietly, looking over at the king now and again and nodding. He was Levi Bell, the lawyer who’d gone to Louisville. Another was a big, rough, powerful fellow who had come up and heard everything the old gentleman said, and was now attending to the king.
